title: What Mississippi Still Hasn't Explained About Nolan Wells' Death

 What Mississippi Still Hasn't Explained About Nolan Wells' Death
 Wayne Ince 
 Oct 31, 2026 
 6 min read 
 They found a wound on the back of his head. Then they closed the case.
 -->
 Add LEVEL on Google 
 The bruise on the back of Nolan Wells’ head measured twelve inches by eight. His mother’s independent pathologist confirmed it was blood, from a blow delivered within about four hours of the eighteen-year-old’s death. Then a Mississippi grand jury looked at that wound and everything around it and decided the State did not need to know how it got there.
 Start with the paperwork, because that's where they lost the plot. Both the state’s own chief medical examiner and Dr. Roger A. Mitchell Jr., the forensic pathologist Nolan’s family hired, ruled the cause and manner of death undetermined. That is the official finding. Undetermined. Then District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath posted a redacted grand jury report to Facebook, calling the death consistent with drowning, and according to Mississippi Today, she texted Nolan’s mother shortly before she did it. “ Consistent with drowning" is a phrase a prosecutor types on social media. Two doctors signed their names to the document. And undetermined is not a shrug. It is the exact finding a medical examiner reaches for when the body will not give up a clean answer. Which is why it should have held this case open, not closed it.
 The word is doing all the work 
 The grand jury called drowning a diagnosis by exclusion. I sat with that phrase for a while. Diagnosis by exclusion means you rule out every other cause until one is left standing. You do not get to skip the hard one. And the hard one here is a fresh injury to the back of a young man’s skull. Liza Park, on the family’s legal team, explained why the timing is nailed down. Nolan’s body had bled at the site but had not yet produced the white blood cells that show up hours later, which puts the blow within about four hours of death. Mitchell wrote it in the language of his trade: a recent antemortem injury within the first few hours. Ben Crump said it in plain English. All other causes must be ruled out prior to certifying a death as drowning. They never ruled out the bruise. They wrote around it.
 Here is the part that ought to stop everyone cold. The state’s own autopsy found no water in Nolan’s lungs, airway, or stomach. Park read it straight off the report. No water in the stomach, no water in the lungs, no water in the throat. I want to be careful with that, because a forensic pathologist will tell you empty lungs do not by themselves rule out drowning, and after two days in the Gulf, water can wash out of a body. Dr. Priya Banerjee made that exact point in Los Angeles Magazine. Fair enough. But follow it forward. The medical examiner had a young man with a fresh head wound and no water in his lungs, and still could not certify how he died. Undetermined. Then a grand jury took the same body and called it drowning anyway. The empty lungs are not proof of a crime. They are one more thing the State could not square and stopped trying to.
 There were three more bruises too, on his lower back and near his left shoulder blade, none of them in the preliminary autopsy. TMZ and The Grio both reported the additions. So the second examination found injuries the first one missed, and the response to that was too close the case, not open it wider.
 Run the tape the other way 
 Nolan Wells was the only Black person in the group that boated to Horn Island on the Fourth of July. PBS reported that everyone else on those boats is white. I am not accusing any of those young men of a crime. No court has; the grand jury found no credible evidence of criminal conduct by the people on the boats named the Triton, the Palm Beach, and the Tideline, and their lawyers have made it loud and litigious that saying otherwise invites a lawsuit. Understood. This piece is not about them. It is about the investigation, and whether the investigation runs the same for a Black kid as it would for a white one.
 So run it the other way. Picture a white eighteen-year-old pulled from the water two days after a holiday boat trip, a fresh twelve-by-eight-inch bruise on the back of his head, and the only kids who came home without him were Black. Imagine the medical examiner writing undetermined. Picture his phone riding back to the mainland on the boat without him. Imagine a grand jury declaring it a drowning and a district attorney shutting down the case on Facebook.
 You already know that a case does not close. You know it in your gut. There are arrests before the funeral. And the specifics earn the intuition. The first autopsy missed three bruises the independent exam found, and the family did not receive the state’s own report until the night of September twenty-third, after the case was already closed. That is what unequal rigor looks like in practice, not in theory. Mississippi Today reported that this case sparked discussion about the state’s history of investigators not examining the deaths of Black people with the same rigor they bring to the deaths of white people. That is not name-calling. That is the reporting, and Mississippi wrote the history it is quoting from.
 I spent twenty-three years in the Air Force. I have watched the military run an investigation into the ground because a family needed to know exactly what happened to their son, down to the last detail, and undetermined is not something you can bury a child with. Christine Wonsley, Nolan’s mother, asked the only question that matters. How can a jury conclude of drowning, she said, despite knowing that there was trauma to his body, and despite hearing many inconsistencies? A week later, nobody has answered her.
 A finished case that keeps arguing with itself 
 McIlrath wants this settled. The information I have released to the public is true and accurate, and I stand by it, she said, and she told the family’s side to stop playing games. Maybe she believes every word. But look at what is still in open dispute a week after she declared the matter closed.
 The family’s digital forensics firm, Garrett Discovery, says Nolan’s phone stayed on the boat and that messages were deleted from it. McIlrath says those deletions came from other Snapchat users on their own devices, not from anyone physically touching Nolan’s phone, and that her office received about three hundred pages of selected findings rather than the full extraction. The two sides cannot even agree on who called off the joint examination of the phone. WLOX reported that Crump’s team did not receive the state’s own autopsy report until the night of September twenty-third, after the case was already closed. That is what a finished investigation looks like now. Two forensic teams talking past each other in dueling press conferences while a mother waits for a straight answer.
 What should happen next? 
 None of this requires believing a crime occurred. It requires refusing to accept an undetermined verdict.
 Mississippi reopens the investigation and brings in an outside medical examiner with no stake in defending the first autopsy, because the office that missed three bruises does not get to grade its own paper. The Department of Justice is opening a civil rights review, which is exactly what Crump has asked for, so the question of whether this death got investigated the way a white child’s would have gets answered by someone who does not live in Jackson County. I know what the odds of that are under this Justice Department, and I am asking anyway. A principle that only holds when it is convenient was never a principle. And they released the records. All of them. The full grand jury materials, the complete phone extraction, the sheriff’s file and the emails between the DA and the family’s attorneys.
 McIlrath says the truth is on her side. Then she loses nothing by laying it on the table where the rest of us can read it. Sunlight is not an accusation. It is the floor, the least you owe a boy who cannot speak for himself. It is also the fastest way to clear the young men who came home. If the full record shows what their attorneys say it shows, releasing it ends the speculation instead of feeding it. The silence is what fuels suspicion. Transparency ends it.
 I do not know how Nolan Wells died. That is the honest sentence, and it is also the charge. Neither does the State of Mississippi, and the State stopped short. Not for lack of hours. A grand jury heard from forty-three witnesses and issued a hundred and thirty-two subpoenas, and I will not pretend that is nothing. It is a lot of work. The State has not completed it. They would not take the last step the evidence demanded, ruling out the fresh wound on the back of his head before certifying a drowning by exclusion. They did everything except the one thing that mattered, then closed the book. That is not laziness. It is a choice. And the report that choice produced tells a grieving mother, in so many words, we will never know. She is not built to accept that. Neither is Ben Crump. And no parent reading this, of any color, should accept a system that finds a fresh wound on the back of a child’s head and rules the wound not worth explaining.
 Say his name until they explain it. Nolan Xavier Wells.
